verba tabulae astronomicae f. 266v praemissa ἐποίησα δὲ τοῦτο εἰς τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ
͵ςωνδʹ ἔτους ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου, ψιεʹ δὲ ἔτει τῶν Περσῶν i. e. anno 1346 p. C.
In capitulo quoque σμγʹ, f. 226v, de anno ͵ςωμηʹ, loqui videtur, qui annus 1390
esset, quo alteram partem huius libri exaratam esse censeo.
Haec autem collectio diversis constat partibus. 1o Capita, quae ex collectaneis
graecis saec. XI, qualia e. g. in codice Venet. 7 et in Parisino 2506 exstant (Catal.
Venet., p. 37, n. 1), Eleutherius hausit. Vide cap. κγʹ, quo exemplum anni ͵ςφογʹ
1075 affertur, cap. σμαʹ ubi genitura anni 1040 praebetur, capp. ιεʹ ss., etc.
2o Capita quae ex diversis operibus persicis vel arabicis nuper in graecam
linguam versis excerpsit, nempe ex Achmetis introductione astrologica
(ff. 158 ss. = cod. Venet. 5, ff. 202 ss.) vel libris qui Persarum vocantur
(capp, ρλαʹ, ρνʹ, ρνεʹ, cf. eundem cod. Venet. 5), ex libro scientiae astronomicae
eorundem Persarum (ff. 214 ss., cap. σλʹ, cf. cod. Mediol. 11. ff. 18 ss.) et aliis.
3o Capita quaedam ff. 268-279, Hermetis, Lydi et syntagmatis quod vocamus
Laurentianum, quo Eleutherius in codice quoque Taurinensi 4 usus est (Catal.
Ital., p. 5, n. 1),
4o Opera quorum Claudius Ptolemaeus auctor fuit vel fuisse credebatur
(ff. 297v-335, cf. cod. Vindobon. 4).
sections.en: the words of the astronomical table f. 266v prefixed 'I made this at the beginning of the year 6854 from the creation of the world, and in the 715th year of the Persians' i. e. in the year 1346 A.D. In chapter 243 also, f. 226v, he seems to speak of the year 6898, which year would be 1390, in which I think the other part of this book was written. But this collection consists of diverse parts. 1st Chapters, which Eleutherius drew from Greek miscellanies of the 11th century, such as exist e. g. in codex Venet. 7 and in Parisinus 2506 (Catal. Venet., p. 37, n. 1). See ch. 23, where an example of the year 6573 (1075) is brought forward, ch. 241 where a nativity of the year 1040 is provided, chs. 15 ff., etc. 2nd Chapters which he excerpted from diverse Persian or Arabic works recently translated into the Greek language, namely from Achmet's astrological introduction (ff. 158 ff. = cod. Venet. 5, ff. 202 ff.) or the books which are called of the Persians (chs. 131, 150, 155, cf. the same cod. Venet. 5), from the book of astronomical science of the same Persians (ff. 214 ff., ch. 230, cf. cod. Mediol. 11. ff. 18 ff.) and others. 3rd Certain chapters ff. 268-279, of Hermes, Lydus and the treatise which we call Laurentian, which Eleutherius also used in codex Taurinensis 4 (Catal. Ital., p. 5, n. 1), 4th Works of which Claudius Ptolemy was the author or was believed to have been (ff. 297v-335, cf. cod. Vindobon. 4).

summary.headline: Astrological Chapters 1–10
summary.text: Chapter list from folios 152v–154v covering death timing, lunar nodes, fleeing women, partnerships, travel, friendship and enmity, lifespan diagnosis, royal gifts, hidden treasure, and the quality of discovered things, with parallels to other codices. An apparatus note attributes the collection to diverse Greek, Persian, Arabic, Hermetic, Lydian, Laurentian, and Ptolemaic materials used by Eleutherius.
